landscape_summary: UQ for molecular property/activity prediction is a crowded space, but the sub-problems cluster into a few well-worked areas and a couple of genuine holes. WELL-WORKED (treat as baselines/kill-list, not contributions): (a) conformal prediction (CP) as a formal applicability-domain replacement and QSAR interval method (Xu 2023 arXiv:2304.00970; Oršolić 2023 Bioinformatics 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad465; CPSign 2024 10.1186/s13321-024-00870-9); (b) CP coverage collapse under scaffold/covariate shift and weighted/density-ratio fixes (CoDrug 2023 arXiv:2310.12033; KMM-CP 2026 arXiv:2603.26415; temporal recalibration Morger 2022 10.1038/s41598-022-09309-3); (c) conformal SELECTION with FDR control for compound prioritisation — now published IN JCIM (Bai 2025 10.1021/acs.jcim.5c01633), with the general ML machinery mature (Jin & Candès 2022 arXiv:2210.01408, 2023 arXiv:2307.09291; MCCS 2025 arXiv:2510.08075; SCoRE 2026 arXiv:2603.24704); (d) Venn-ABERS/probability calibration (Mervin 2020 10.1021/acs.jcim.0c00476); (e) class-conditional Mondrian fixing minority under-coverage (Tursunbadalov 2026 arXiv:2607.06605); (f) a sharp negative result showing selective-prediction abstention tracks local label variance not novelty and does NOT beat point-ranking for prioritisation (Srivastava & Kassetty 2026 arXiv:2611.01512). THE CLEAREST OPEN HOLE is censored/qualified labels meeting conformal methods. Censored activity labels are ~24% of ChEMBL potency records (NeurIPS 2026 abstract, unverified), and the pharma-ML community has attacked TRAINING with them (Tobit UQ: Svensson 2025 10.1016/j.ailsci.2025.100128; temporal shift: Friesacher 2025 10.1016/j.ailsci.2025.100132) — but NOT conformal calibration/selection. Meanwhile all conformal-censored theory lives in survival analysis with random RIGHT-censoring (Candès 2021 arXiv:2103.09763; Gui/Barber 2022 arXiv:2211.01227; Sesia & Svetnik 2024 arXiv:2412.09729; Holmes & Marandon 2024 arXiv:2410.24136), a different regime from molecular assay censoring, which is type-I-like (threshold known for every record) and typically one-sided at a detection/solubility limit. No one has asked: what happens to CP coverage, to interval width, or to FDR-controlled hit selection when the CALIBRATION labels themselves are bounds? Naive practice silently drops ~a quarter of data or imputes bounds as exact, both of which should break the guarantee. This gap is precise, testable, strongly baselined, multi-dataset (ChEMBL native qualifiers + semi-synthetic censoring on 15-22 TDC/MoleculeNet regression sets), CPU-cheap (fingerprints + LightGBM/sklearn), and defensible on validity/efficiency/decision-quality even if point accuracy only ties. Two secondary holes are also viable: new-group (unseen-scaffold-cluster) coverage via hierarchical exchangeability (theory exists — Lee/Barber/Willett 2023 arXiv:2306.06342 — but untested on chemotypes), and a practical-significance, multi-dataset audit (per Ash 2025 10.1021/acs.jcim.5c01609) of whether any UQ signal improves downstream decisions over point-ranking, generalising Srivastava's 2-dataset negative result.

candidates.title: Censoring-aware conformal prediction for molecular activity: valid intervals when the calibration labels are qualified (>/<)
candidates.problem: In real bioactivity data a large fraction of potency labels are censored (reported as '>X' or '<X' at an assay detection/solubility limit, not an exact value). Split conformal prediction assumes every calibration point yields a computable nonconformity score |y-yhat|, which a bound does not. Practitioners therefore either drop censored rows (discarding ~a quarter of data, and non-randomly — censoring correlates with inactivity/edge-of-range) or impute the bound as an exact value. Both silently violate the exchangeability/scoring assumptions that CP's coverage guarantee rests on, yet no cheminformatics work quantifies the damage or offers a principled calibration under censoring.
candidates.what_exists: Conformal regression for QSAR with exact labels (Xu 2023 arXiv:2304.00970; CPSign 2024). Training-side censored-label methods: Tobit-based UQ (Svensson 2025 10.1016/j.ailsci.2025.100128) and temporal-shift UQ (Friesacher 2025 10.1016/j.ailsci.2025.100132) — both learn from bounds but evaluate point/UQ accuracy, never conformal calibration. Conformal theory for censoring exists only in survival analysis with random right-censoring (Candès 2021 arXiv:2103.09763; Gui/Barber 2022 arXiv:2211.01227; Sesia & Svetnik 2024 arXiv:2412.09729; Holmes & Marandon 2024 arXiv:2410.24136; two-sided Tobit label-shift Choi 2026 arXiv:2607.02173). A NeurIPS 2026 abstract quantifies ~24% censoring in ChEMBL 36 but studies point RMSE, not intervals (unverified).
candidates.gap: No method, and no benchmark, for split-conformal interval construction whose finite-sample coverage is preserved (or provably conservative) when a known fraction of the CALIBRATION set carries one-sided type-I-censored (threshold-known) labels — the regime that actually characterises molecular assays, as opposed to survival's random right-censoring. The distinction matters: molecular censoring thresholds are observed for every record, enabling exact partial-order scoring rather than IPCW imputation.
candidates.proposed_contribution: A 'partial-order / interval-score' conformal calibration: for a right-censored active ('>X') the true nonconformity |y-yhat| is only known to lie in [max(0, X-yhat), inf) when yhat<X, and is a computable point when yhat>X; symmetric for left-censored. Treat each censored calibration score as a one-sided interval and take the conservative (coverage-safe) quantile over the resulting partially-ordered score set — provably >= nominal coverage with no distributional assumption, degrading gracefully to standard split CP at 0% censoring. Compare against (i) drop-censored, (ii) impute-at-threshold, (iii) impute-Tobit-conditional-mean, (iv) treat-bound-as-exact. Provide a one-sided-interval variant (lower predictive bound for actives, the decision-relevant quantity) and a Mondrian variant stratified by censoring status.
candidates.hypothesis: As censoring fraction rises, drop-censored and impute-as-exact calibration lose coverage monotonically (PICP falls below 1-alpha, biased because censored points are non-exchangeable with exact ones), whereas the partial-order calibration maintains >= nominal coverage at the cost of modestly wider intervals; crucially it keeps intervals tighter than the trivially-conservative 'drop + widen' approach, and recovers more usable (non-infinite) lower bounds for actives.

'Does it beat impute-as-exact in practice?' — the controlled semi-synthetic sweep answers this with ground-truth coverage. 'Accuracy doesn't improve' — the contribution is validity + usable-bound efficiency + decision quality, explicitly defensible under a tie, matching JCIM's method-comparison guidance.

candidates.title: Conformal hit-selection with FDR control that uses, rather than discards, censored calibration labels
candidates.problem: Conformal selection prioritises compounds with FDR control but its p-values require nonconformity scores on a labelled calibration set. When calibration actives are reported as '>X' (right-censored), the standard construction cannot score them, so pipelines drop them — exactly the high-potency compounds most informative for selecting more actives. This both wastes data and can bias the FDR guarantee if the dropped set is non-exchangeable.
candidates.what_exists: Conformal selection with FDR control is published in JCIM for compound screening with EXACT labels (Bai et al. 2025 10.1021/acs.jcim.5c01633; machinery: Jin & Candès 2022 arXiv:2210.01408; weighted/covariate-shift Jin & Candès 2023 arXiv:2307.09291; optimised scores Bai & Jin 2024 arXiv:2411.17983; multi-condition MCCS 2025 arXiv:2510.08075; general risk SCoRE 2026 arXiv:2603.24704). None handles censored calibration labels.
candidates.gap: No conformal-selection procedure that incorporates censored (qualified) calibration labels while retaining finite-sample FDR control. A '>X' active gives a one-sided bound on its calibration score, which can be used conservatively to build valid (possibly conservative) conformal p-values instead of discarding the record.
candidates.proposed_contribution: Define censoring-robust conformal p-values: for selecting compounds with activity above threshold c, a calibration active censored at '>X' with X>=c is a certain-positive whose score bound tightens (not loosens) the p-value; one censored below contributes a conservative score. Prove FDR control via the exchangeability of the conservative scores (BH on conformal p-values). Deliver a drop-in extension of Bai 2025 that is never anti-conservative and recovers power by retaining censored actives.
candidates.hypothesis: At matched target FDR, the censoring-aware selector achieves strictly higher power (more true actives selected / larger valid batch) than the drop-censored selector, with empirical FDR at or below nominal across datasets; the gap widens with censoring fraction.

candidates.title: Does any uncertainty signal improve molecular decisions over point-ranking? A 15+ dataset practical-significance audit of calibration provenance and selective prioritisation
candidates.problem: CP and selective prediction are promoted as decision tools for prioritisation and abstention, but recent evidence suggests the UQ signal may add nothing over ranking by the point prediction, and that coverage validity depends more on where the calibration set comes from (random vs scaffold vs temporal) than on the method. These claims exist only at small scale (1-2 datasets, single model) and have not been subjected to the field's own practical-significance standards.
candidates.what_exists: Srivastava & Kassetty 2026 (arXiv:2611.01512): on 2 datasets, 1 GBDT model, abstention tracks local label variance not novelty, width/variance gating never beats point-ranking for hit precision, and conformal coverage hinges on calibration provenance. Temporal coverage loss + recalibration (Morger 2022 10.1038/s41598-022-09309-3). Practical-significance method-comparison protocol (Ash 2025 10.1021/acs.jcim.5c01609). Benchmarks of UQ accuracy (MUBen 2023 arXiv:2306.10060) but keyed to calibration error, not decision quality.
candidates.gap: No large-scale, protocol-grade test of the decision-usefulness of UQ (CP, Venn-ABERS, ensemble variance, AD) for compound prioritisation and abstention, nor a systematic map of how calibration provenance (random/scaffold-cluster/temporal) controls realised coverage and FDR across many datasets.
candidates.proposed_contribution: An evaluation-validity paper: across >=15 datasets, >=3 model families, and 3 calibration-provenance regimes, measure (a) realised coverage/FDR vs nominal, (b) whether gating/abstaining on each UQ signal improves decision metrics (precision@budget, BEDROC, enrichment) over point-ranking, with practical-significance effect sizes and correct paired statistics per Ash 2025. Deliver a reusable, CPU-only benchmark and a decision-rule recommendation (when UQ helps, when ranking suffices).
candidates.hypothesis: Marginal CP coverage is systematically optimistic under scaffold/temporal calibration and restored only by matched-provenance calibration; and UQ-based gating yields no practically-significant improvement over point-ranking for prioritisation on most datasets, with gains concentrated in high-shift, small-budget regimes.

candidates.title: Coverage for unseen chemotypes: hierarchical/Mondrian conformal prediction with new-group guarantees over scaffold clusters
candidates.problem: Lead optimisation asks for reliable prediction on chemical series NOT represented in training (new scaffold clusters). Marginal CP guarantees only average coverage and demonstrably under-covers novel groups; within-group Mondrian only helps groups seen at calibration time. The relevant object — coverage for a test point from a brand-new group — needs group-level (hierarchical) exchangeability, which has theory but no cheminformatics instantiation.
candidates.what_exists: Hierarchical-exchangeability distribution-free inference with new-group coverage (Lee, Barber, Willett 2023 arXiv:2306.06342; two-layer Dunn/Wasserman/Ramdas 2018 arXiv:1809.07441). Molecular Mondrian/group-conditional CP for SEEN groups (DTI: Rakhshaninejad 2025 arXiv:2505.18890). Overlapping-group coverage (Kandinsky 2025 arXiv:2502.17264). Minority class-conditional fix (Tursunbadalov 2026 arXiv:2607.06605). Covariate-shift scaffold fixes (CoDrug 2023 arXiv:2310.12033; KMM-CP 2026 arXiv:2603.26415).
candidates.gap: No application of hierarchical-exchangeability new-group CP to molecular scaffold clusters, and no benchmark of whether treating scaffold clusters as exchangeable groups yields valid coverage for held-out clusters (unseen chemotypes) at tolerable interval width.
candidates.proposed_contribution: Cast Bemis-Murcko / Butina scaffold clusters as exchangeable groups; apply split hierarchical CP (calibrate at the group level) to produce intervals with coverage for a test molecule from an unseen cluster; compare marginal, within-group Mondrian, covariate-shift-weighted, and hierarchical constructions; characterise the width/validity trade-off and when scaffold clusters are 'exchangeable enough'.
candidates.hypothesis: Marginal and seen-group Mondrian CP under-cover held-out scaffold clusters; hierarchical-exchangeability CP restores >= nominal cluster-level coverage at the cost of wider intervals, and does so more reliably than covariate-shift weighting when support overlap is poor.

candidates.title: Conditional-coverage recovery at activity cliffs via roughness/AD-conditioned Mondrian conformal prediction, with guarantees, on 30 MoleculeACE sets
candidates.problem: Standard calibrated UQ gives valid marginal coverage but fails exactly on activity cliffs (near-identical molecules, large potency gaps), because popular reliability signals are organised around distance-to-training-data and cliffs are close to training data. Clinicians/chemists most need reliability precisely at these mispredictions.
candidates.what_exists: A Research Square preprint (rs-10071162, UNVERIFIED) reports that RF-variance, AD, and Sheridan estimators are at-chance for cliffs on 30 MoleculeACE targets, proposes a neighbour-based roughness measure (median ROC-AUC ~0.69) and roughness-conditioned CP intervals that stabilise coverage. MoleculeACE benchmark (van Tilborg 2022 10.1021/acs.jcim.2c01073). AD-vs-uncertainty link (Hosni 2026 10.1021/acsomega.5c11875). dAD local CP (Oršolić 2023 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad465). Mondrian class-conditional (Tursunbadalov 2026 arXiv:2607.06605).
candidates.gap: The roughness-CP idea is only a single unverified preprint with no formal coverage framing, no comparison to Mondrian-conditioned-on-roughness with guarantees, and no decision-quality evaluation. Whether conditioning CP on a cliff/roughness variable yields valid GROUP-conditional coverage (not just stabilised marginal coverage) across many datasets is open.
candidates.proposed_contribution: Formalise cliff-aware CP as Mondrian CP with bins defined by a local-roughness / AD score (and combinations), delivering group-conditional coverage guarantees for cliff vs smooth regions; benchmark against marginal CP, variance-normalised CP, and AD-conditioned CP on all 30 MoleculeACE sets; report both coverage and whether cliff-flagging improves any downstream decision.
candidates.hypothesis: Roughness-binned Mondrian CP achieves near-nominal coverage within the cliff bin where marginal and variance-normalised CP under-cover, at a modest width cost, and roughness outperforms AD/variance as the conditioning variable for cliff coverage.

landscape_summary: The 2022-2026 literature on data quality and evaluation validity in molecular ML has converged on a clear message: reported accuracy gains on standard benchmarks are frequently smaller than, or confounded by, irreducible label noise, split artefacts, and leakage. Three strands anchor the field. (1) Noise quantification: Landrum & Riniker (JCIM 2024, 10.1021/acs.jcim.4c00049) show combining IC50/Ki across assays injects large noise (65% of points differ >0.3 log with minimal curation; Kendall tau ~0.51); Crusius, Cipcigan & Biggin (Faraday Discuss. 2025, 10.1039/d4fd00091a) derive per-dataset performance ceilings from assumed experimental error and release NoiseEstimator, finding several popular datasets may already be at/above their noise ceiling; Nelen et al. (J Cheminform 2025, 10.1186/s13321-025-00956-y) show matched pairs are more robust to inter-assay variance. (2) Evaluation protocol: Ash, Wognum et al. (JCIM 2025, 10.1021/acs.jcim.5c01609) lay out practically-significant method-comparison protocols (repeated splits, paired tests, effect sizes, Polaris tooling) — now the expected standard for JCIM method papers. (3) Split/leakage validity: audits of LIT-PCBA (arXiv 2507.21404) and emerging ADMET near-duplicate censuses show random and even scaffold splits leak near-duplicates and inflate scores; SIMPD (J Cheminform 2023, 10.1186/s13321-023-00787-9) offers simulated temporal splits (99 ChEMBL datasets). Censored labels are contested: Svensson et al. (AILS 2025, 10.1016/j.ailsci.2025.100128) argue Tobit-style modelling improves UQ, while a NeurIPS 2026 submission reports Tobit hurts naive regression on linear-IC50 rows — an open empirical question. Pairwise/delta learning (DeepDelta, J Cheminform 2023, 10.1186/s13321-023-00769-x; DeltaClassifier, RSC Med Chem 2024, 10.1039/d4md00325j) claims large small-data gains, but its evaluation (every test pair scored, implicit augmentation) has unresolved leakage and fairness questions. Activity cliffs (MoleculeACE, van Tilborg 2022) are intrinsically pairwise yet scored per-compound. The common thread and opportunity: contributions that remain defensible on an accuracy tie — noise-normalised leaderboards, leakage-corrected and pairwise-correct metrics, calibration/coverage guarantees under realistic splits, and decision-quality rather than RMSE. Several adjacent ideas (ADMET leakage census, censored-label census) are already appearing at NeurIPS 2026, so positioning must avoid those exact framings. All proposals below use only public data already cached locally (TDC ADMET 22 datasets; MoleculeACE 30 ChEMBL activity-cliff sets) plus optional ChEMBL REST, and fit 4 CPU / 15 GB / <=15 h with RDKit + LightGBM/XGBoost/sklearn and small CPU GNNs.

candidates.title: Noise-ceiling-normalised leaderboards: how much of the molecular-ML ranking survives when you divide out the irreducible label noise?
candidates.problem: Benchmark leaderboards (TDC ADMET, MoleculeACE) rank methods by raw RMSE/Spearman, but the achievable ceiling differs per dataset because experimental/replicate noise differs per assay. A 0.02 RMSE gap on a high-noise assay and a low-noise assay are not comparable, yet both are reported identically. No multi-dataset study has (a) estimated the ceiling empirically from replicate/assay variance per dataset and (b) re-ranked a full method pool against that ceiling using a rigorous paired protocol.
candidates.what_exists: Crusius et al. (Faraday Discuss. 2025) derive ceilings but for only 9 datasets, using an *assumed* sigma_E injected as synthetic noise, and do not re-rank a method pool. Landrum & Riniker (JCIM 2024) measure real inter-assay noise but on curation, not on leaderboard normalisation. Ash/Wognum (JCIM 2025) give the comparison protocol but not noise-normalisation. Brown et al. earlier proposed the noise-injection idea.
candidates.gap: No work (i) estimates per-dataset noise ceilings empirically (ChEMBL replicate pairs for activity sets; literature sigma_E priors for ADMET) across >=15 datasets, (ii) expresses each method's score as a fraction-of-ceiling-closed metric, and (iii) tests, with the Ash paired/effect-size protocol, whether the method *ranking* and the claimed 'practically significant' gaps survive normalisation. The testable claim 'most reported ADMET/cliff method gains lie within the per-dataset noise band' has never been quantified at scale.
candidates.proposed_contribution: A reproducible protocol + open leaderboard that (1) estimates a per-dataset noise ceiling: for the 30 MoleculeACE ChEMBL targets, pull replicate measurements of the same compound-target from ChEMBL REST to get sigma_E empirically; for TDC ADMET use literature/curation-based sigma_E priors and the NoiseEstimator noise-injection to get a ceiling distribution. (2) Train a fixed pool of ~6 baselines, report raw score AND ceiling-normalised 'fraction of attainable performance'. (3) Apply the Ash protocol (>=10 repeated splits, paired Wilcoxon, Cohen-style effect sizes, practical-significance thresholds) to both raw and normalised scores, reporting how many pairwise method comparisons flip from 'significant' to 'within noise'. Deliver a NoiseEstimator-compatible package and per-dataset ceiling table.
candidates.hypothesis: H1: After ceiling-normalisation, a large fraction (>50%) of previously 'significant' pairwise method differences on ADMET/MoleculeACE become statistically or practically indistinguishable. H2: Datasets differ enough in ceiling that the *same* absolute RMSE gap is practically significant on some and noise on others, so a single global ranking is misleading.

candidates.title: Leakage-controlled, compute-matched re-evaluation of pairwise/delta learning: when does predicting property *differences* actually beat predicting values?
candidates.problem: Delta/pairwise models (DeepDelta, DeltaClassifier) report large small-data gains by training on all O(n^2) molecule pairs and predicting property differences. But their evaluation scores every test pair, and nearest-neighbour pairs span the train/test boundary, so claimed gains may be partly an evaluation artefact (implicit augmentation, pair-level leakage) rather than a real modelling advantage. The conditions under which delta genuinely helps are unquantified.
candidates.what_exists: DeepDelta (J Cheminform 2023) and DeltaClassifier (RSC Med Chem 2024) show delta beats absolute RF/Chemprop on ADMET/potency, especially small data and cliffs. Nelen et al. (2025) show matched pairs are noise-robust, supporting the pairwise premise. No study controls pair-level leakage or matches training compute/pair budget between absolute and delta models.
candidates.gap: A fair, leakage-audited comparison is missing: (i) absolute vs delta under identical wall-clock/pair budgets, (ii) delta evaluated with and without pairs that cross the split boundary, (iii) decision-quality metrics (correct ranking of analogues within a series) rather than only pair-RMSE, across many datasets. The open question of whether delta's advantage is a modelling gain or an evaluation inflation has not been resolved.
candidates.proposed_contribution: A protocol that (1) defines three pairing regimes for test evaluation: all-pairs (original), train-anchored-only, and within-test-only; (2) reports how the delta-vs-absolute gap changes across regimes to isolate the augmentation/leakage component; (3) matches compute by capping delta training pairs to the absolute model's budget; (4) adds lead-optimisation decision metrics: within-scaffold-series ranking (Kendall tau), top-k analogue selection accuracy, and sign-of-change accuracy. Delivered across 30 MoleculeACE + selected ADMET regression sets.
candidates.hypothesis: H1: A measurable fraction of delta's reported RMSE advantage disappears when test pairs are restricted to train-anchored (leakage-controlled) pairing. H2: Delta's residual advantage concentrates in small-data and activity-cliff regimes and in *ranking* decisions, not in global value regression — i.e. delta is a prioritisation tool, not an accuracy tool.

candidates.title: Does censoring-aware training help or hurt across splits? A multi-dataset, split-stratified resolution of the Tobit controversy
candidates.problem: A quarter of ChEMBL potency labels are qualified/censored (>, <). Pipelines often silently drop them or treat them as exact. Whether censoring-aware (Tobit/survival) training improves regression and uncertainty is actively contradicted in the literature, with no multi-dataset, split-stratified arbitration.
candidates.what_exists: Svensson et al. (AILS 2025) adapt ensembles/Bayesian/GP with a Tobit likelihood and report better UQ when using censored labels. A NeurIPS 2026 submission reports Tobit *hurts* naive regression (+0.108 log units worse) on identical linear-IC50 rows across 156 targets. DeltaClassifier (RSC Med Chem 2024) exploits bounded points for classification. Mervin's Probabilistic RF (J Cheminform 2021, 10.1186/s13321-021-00539-7) handles experimental uncertainty near thresholds.
candidates.gap: The contradiction is unresolved because the two camps use different tasks (UQ vs point regression), scales (pIC50 vs linear IC50), and split schemes. No study varies the censored fraction, the split (random/scaffold/SIMPD-temporal), and the downstream objective (point accuracy vs calibrated UQ vs decision ranking) together across >=15 datasets with real relation fields.
candidates.proposed_contribution: Pull relation-field-aware datasets from ChEMBL REST for ~15-20 targets spanning low-to-high censored fraction. Compare four label policies: drop-censored, impute-at-threshold, Tobit/censored-likelihood regression (LightGBM with a censored objective or a CPU Gaussian/ensemble Tobit), and DeltaClassifier-style pairwise sign. Stratify by split (random, scaffold, SIMPD temporal where available) and by censored fraction. Report when each policy wins on point accuracy, calibration/coverage, and decision ranking. Produce a decision chart: 'given censored fraction f and split type, use policy X'.
candidates.hypothesis: H1: Tobit helps calibration/UQ and decision ranking but not necessarily point RMSE, reconciling the two camps (task-dependent). H2: The benefit of keeping censored labels grows with censored fraction and under temporal/scaffold splits (where extrapolation makes bounds informative) and vanishes under random splits.

candidates.title: A pairwise, leakage-audited activity-cliff metric: fixing how MoleculeACE scores what is fundamentally a pair problem
candidates.problem: Activity cliffs are defined on *pairs* of similar molecules with large potency differences, yet MoleculeACE scores them with per-compound RMSE_cliff (a compound is flagged if it belongs to any cliff). This conflates which pair is mispredicted, ignores whether the model gets the *direction* and *magnitude* of the cliff, and the official splits may place near-duplicate cliff partners on both sides, leaking the answer.
candidates.what_exists: MoleculeACE (van Tilborg et al., JCIM 2022) benchmarks 30 targets with per-compound RMSE_cliff and binary cliff membership. GraphCliff (arXiv 2511.03170, 2025) and others still report per-compound RMSE_cliff on the official split. LIT-PCBA audits (arXiv 2507.21404) show near-duplicate leakage inflates other benchmarks. No one has audited MoleculeACE splits for cliff-partner leakage or replaced the metric with a pairwise one.
candidates.gap: Missing: (i) a near-duplicate/cliff-partner leakage audit of MoleculeACE's official splits (are both members of a cliff pair separated across train/test, and how often is a test cliff compound's partner in train?), and (ii) a pairwise cliff metric that scores direction + magnitude of each cliff pair (cliff-pair ranking AUC, sign accuracy, delta-magnitude error) rather than per-compound RMSE. The field evaluates a pair phenomenon with a point metric on possibly-leaky splits.
candidates.proposed_contribution: (1) Enumerate all cliff pairs per MoleculeACE dataset via RDKit (fingerprint/scaffold/SMILES similarity >=0.9 and >10x potency), audit how official train/test splits distribute pair members and compute per-dataset partner-leakage rate. (2) Define pairwise cliff metrics: cliff-pair sign accuracy, cliff-pair ranking (does the model order the pair correctly), and delta-magnitude MAE. (3) Re-benchmark the standard method pool under (a) official vs (b) a cliff-pair-disjoint split, reporting how rankings and absolute cliff performance change; include a 1-NN memorisation control to expose leakage. Release the pairwise metric + cliff-disjoint splits.
candidates.hypothesis: H1: MoleculeACE official splits leak cliff partners for a non-trivial fraction of test cliffs, and a parameter-free 1-NN model achieves deceptively strong RMSE_cliff because of it. H2: Under the pairwise, leakage-controlled protocol, apparent method differences on cliffs shrink and the per-compound RMSE_cliff ranking does not match the pairwise-ranking ranking, so the current metric misranks methods for the task practitioners care about.

candidates.title: Calibration is the missing leaderboard axis: conformal coverage under scaffold, cluster, and SIMPD-temporal splits as a first-class, noise-referenced benchmark
candidates.problem: Leaderboards rank by point accuracy, but deployed models need calibrated uncertainty for triage decisions. Standard conformal prediction assumes exchangeability, which realistic chemical splits (scaffold, cluster, temporal) violate, silently destroying coverage. No multi-dataset benchmark reports coverage as a headline axis alongside accuracy, nor references the coverage target to the dataset's noise ceiling.
candidates.what_exists: CoDrug (arXiv 2310.12033) shows unweighted conformal under-covers badly under scaffold/fingerprint splits (e.g. 0.34 vs 0.80 target) and density-weighting helps; class-conditional/Mondrian fixes (arXiv 2607.06605) and covariate-shift reweighting (KMM-CP, arXiv 2603.26415) partly recover it. These are mostly single/few-dataset, mostly classification, and not tied to noise ceilings or SIMPD temporal splits.
candidates.gap: Missing: a >=15-dataset regression benchmark that (i) reports conformal coverage and interval efficiency under four splits (random, scaffold, Butina-cluster, SIMPD-temporal), (ii) tests practical CPU-cheap fixes (Mondrian/normalised/Mahalanobis-weighted conformal), and (iii) references the interval width to the per-dataset noise ceiling so that 'well-calibrated' is judged against irreducible noise, not an arbitrary target. Coverage has never been promoted to a leaderboard axis for ADMET regression under temporal splits.
candidates.proposed_contribution: Add calibration as a reported axis: for TDC ADMET regression + MoleculeACE, compute split-conformal coverage and mean interval width under four splits, compare standard vs normalised vs Mahalanobis/KMM-weighted conformal, and report a 'calibration-under-shift' score. Tie interval width to the noise ceiling (shared with candidate A) so over-wide intervals on low-noise data and under-coverage on shifted splits are both visible. Deliver per-dataset coverage tables and a reusable CPU conformal wrapper.
candidates.hypothesis: H1: Under scaffold/cluster/SIMPD splits, marginal conformal under-covers on a majority of datasets; the drop correlates with train/test distribution distance. H2: A cheap normalised/weighted conformal recovers most of the coverage gap at modest interval-width cost, and ranking methods by accuracy alone does not predict their calibration ranking (so calibration adds non-redundant information to the leaderboard).

ranking.title: A pairwise, leakage-audited activity-cliff metric: fixing how MoleculeACE scores what is fundamentally a pair problem
ranking.closest_prior_art_found: MoleculeACE: van Tilborg et al., JCIM 2022, 10.1021/acs.jcim.2c01073 (chemRxiv 10.26434/chemrxiv-2022-mfq52, both verified) defines per-compound RMSE_cliff. Dablander et al., 'Exploring QSAR models for activity-cliff prediction', J Cheminform 2023, 10.1186/s13321-023-00708-w (VERIFIED) does pair-based cliff *prediction* but not a leakage audit of the benchmark splits or a replacement metric. LIT-PCBA leakage template arXiv:2507.21404 (UNVERIFIED) and GraphCliff arXiv:2511.03170 (UNVERIFIED) exist but neither audits MoleculeACE. Targeted searches returned NO existing MoleculeACE cliff-partner leakage audit or pairwise cliff metric. Gap is real.
ranking.rationale: Strongest survivor. Self-contained (30 cached MoleculeACE sets, no external assumptions), cheapest (~5-7h CPU), corrects a highly-cited JCIM benchmark, and is double-hypothesised so it cannot produce a pure null: either partner-leakage exists (headline 1) OR the pairwise metric re-ranks methods vs per-compound RMSE_cliff (headline 2). A parameter-free 1-NN memoriser is almost guaranteed to expose any leakage. Defensible on a tie by construction because the paper IS an evaluation-validity contribution, matching JCIM's stated priorities (Ash 2025). 30 single-family datasets give genuine multi-dataset statistical power.
ranking.sharpened_design: METHOD: (1) Enumerate all cliff pairs per dataset with RDKit (ECFP/scaffold/SMILES sim >=0.9 AND >10x potency, mirroring MoleculeACE's own definition). (2) Audit official 80/20 splits: per-dataset partner-leakage rate = fraction of test cliff compounds whose cliff partner is in train; and a stronger 'near-duplicate' rate (sim>=0.95). (3) Define pairwise cliff metrics on test cliff pairs: sign-of-change accuracy, cliff-pair ranking accuracy (does the model order the pair correctly), delta-magnitude MAE. (4) Build cliff-pair-disjoint splits (both members of every cliff pair forced to the same side) and re-benchmark the pool under official vs disjoint splits. RQs: (RQ1) What is the partner-leakage rate across the 30 sets, and does a 1-NN/scaffold-lookup memoriser achieve deceptively strong RMSE_cliff under official splits? -> leakage audit experiment. (RQ2) Does per-compound RMSE_cliff ranking of the method pool agree with the pairwise-ranking ranking (Kendall tau between rankings)? -> metric-concordance experiment. (RQ3) How much does cliff-pair-disjoint splitting shrink apparent method gaps on cliffs, controlling for reduced training size? -> split-comparison with data-size controls. (RQ4) Does the memoriser control's advantage track the per-dataset leakage rate? -> regression of memoriser-gap on leakage rate. DATASETS: all 30 MoleculeACE ChEMBL sets. BASELINES: Morgan-FP RF / LightGBM / SVR(Tanimoto), one small CPU GNN, 1-NN and scaffold-lookup memorisation controls. ABLATIONS: similarity threshold (0.9/0.95), potency-fold cutoff (10x/100x), FP vs scaffold vs SMILES partner definition, split seed variability. STATS: >=10 repeated splits, paired Wilcoxon with Cohen-style effect sizes and practical-significance thresholds per Ash 2025 (10.1021/acs.jcim.5c01609, VERIFIED); report win/tie/loss and ranking-concordance CIs via bootstrap. DELIVERABLE: open pairwise-cliff metric package + cliff-disjoint splits.

ranking.title: Noise-ceiling-normalised leaderboards: how much of the molecular-ML ranking survives when you divide out irreducible label noise?
ranking.closest_prior_art_found: Crusius, Cipcigan & Biggin, Faraday Discuss. 2025, 10.1039/d4fd00091a (VERIFIED) derives ceilings via noise injection on 9 datasets, releases NoiseEstimator, but does NOT use empirical per-dataset replicate noise at scale nor re-rank a method pool. Landrum & Riniker, JCIM 2024, 10.1021/acs.jcim.4c00049 (VERIFIED) quantifies real inter-assay ChEMBL noise (basis for empirical sigma_E). Ash et al. JCIM 2025 10.1021/acs.jcim.5c01609 (VERIFIED) supplies the protocol. No work combines empirical per-dataset ceilings + full re-ranking + flip-rate across >=15 sets.
ranking.rationale: Close second. Concrete quantitative headline (fraction of 'significant' pairwise gaps that collapse to 'within noise' after ceiling-normalisation) that is virtually guaranteed to be non-trivial. Excellent JCIM fit, CPU-feasible, defensible on a tie. Weaker than D only on dependency risk: ChEMBL replicate sparsity for some targets and the ceiling estimate's own uncertainty create a verification burden, and a reviewer will say it 'extends Crusius.' Mitigated by empirical replicate ceilings + bootstrap CIs + a calibration check that injected noise matches real replicate variance.
ranking.sharpened_design: METHOD: (1) Per-dataset ceiling estimation: for 30 MoleculeACE targets, pull ChEMBL REST replicate measurements of the same compound-target to get empirical sigma_E; for TDC ADMET use Landrum/Riniker-style curation priors + NoiseEstimator injection to get a ceiling distribution with bootstrap CIs. (2) Train a fixed pool of ~6 baselines; report raw score AND ceiling-normalised 'fraction-of-attainable-performance'. (3) Apply Ash protocol to BOTH raw and normalised scores; headline = count of pairwise comparisons that flip from 'significant' to 'within noise'. RQs: (RQ1) Empirical per-dataset ceiling and its CI across >=15 sets -> replicate-pull + injection experiment. (RQ2) What fraction of previously-significant pairwise method differences become indistinguishable after normalisation? -> flip-rate experiment. (RQ3) Does the same absolute RMSE gap flip practical-significance verdict across datasets of differing ceiling? -> cross-dataset effect-size experiment. (RQ4) Do injected-noise ceilings agree with empirical replicate ceilings on the subset where both exist? -> validation experiment. DATASETS: TDC ADMET group (22) + MoleculeACE (30) = up to 52. BASELINES: Morgan-FP+RF, Morgan-FP+LightGBM, RDKit-desc+XGBoost, SVR(Tanimoto), small CPU MPNN (<=20k), k-NN control. ABLATIONS: sigma_E source (empirical vs prior vs injection), replicate-count threshold, target-level vs compound-level sigma_E fallback. STATS: >=10 repeats, paired Wilcoxon + effect sizes (Ash 2025), bootstrap CIs on the ceiling itself and on the flip-rate. COMPUTE: ~8-11h on 4 cores; cache ChEMBL pulls once.

ranking.title: Does censoring-aware training help or hurt across splits? A multi-dataset, split-stratified resolution of the Tobit controversy
ranking.closest_prior_art_found: Svensson et al., AILS 2025, 10.1016/j.ailsci.2025.100128 (VERIFIED) = Tobit helps UQ. NeurIPS 2026 census neurips.cc/virtual/2026/161093 (abstract, UNVERIFIED peer review) = Tobit HURTS point RMSE by 0.108 log units on 156 targets, 'treating bounds as exact saved accuracy.' CensorADMET chemRxiv 10.26434/chemrxiv.15006239 Jul 2026 (VERIFIED exists) already does censored-ADMET training with a tunable deficit budget under scaffold/assay-provenance shift. Fralish DeltaClassifier RSC Med Chem 2024 10.1039/d4md00325j (VERIFIED). The space is crowding fast.
ranking.rationale: The contradiction is real and the split x task x censored-fraction arbitration is a clean, likely-publishable reconciliation ('Tobit helps UQ/ranking, not point RMSE; benefit grows with censoring fraction and under temporal/scaffold splits'). Downgraded to RISKY because CensorADMET + the NeurIPS census now occupy much of this territory, and a custom censored LightGBM objective carries implementation/validation risk. Differentiate via the actionable decision chart and split-stratification, validate the custom Tobit objective against Svensson's published GP numbers on a shared target.
ranking.sharpened_design: METHOD: pull relation-field-aware ChEMBL sets (~15-20 targets spanning 10-55% censoring); compare 4 label policies (drop-censored, impute-at-threshold, Tobit/censored-likelihood LightGBM, DeltaClassifier sign) x 3 splits (random, scaffold, SIMPD temporal via 10.1186/s13321-023-00787-9 VERIFIED). RQs: (RQ1) Does Tobit help calibration/coverage but not point RMSE? -> task-stratified experiment. (RQ2) Does the benefit of keeping censored labels grow with censored fraction? -> fraction-stratified experiment. (RQ3) Does it grow under temporal/scaffold vs random splits? -> split-stratified experiment. (RQ4) Does the custom tree Tobit objective reproduce Svensson GP results on a shared target? -> validation experiment. METRICS: RMSE/MAE on exact-label test points, ECE + conformal coverage, Kendall tau + top-k ranking; Ash paired protocol. COMPUTE ~10-13h.

ranking.title: Censoring-aware conformal prediction for molecular activity: valid intervals when calibration labels are qualified (>/<)
ranking.closest_prior_art_found: Liu, de Paula & Tamer, arXiv:2501.10117 (VERIFIED) 'Prediction Sets and Conformal Inference with Interval Outcomes' is a GENERAL conformal method for left/right/interval-censored outcomes that builds nonconformity scores from interval bounds under fixed bracketing AND random censoring -- this substantially anticipates the proposed 'partial-order/interval-score' construction. Choi arXiv:2607.02173 (VERIFIED) does two-sided Tobit censored conformal via weighted calibration. arXiv:2408.16381 'Uncertainty quantification for intervals' (VERIFIED) does conformal predictive regions for interval-censored targets. Gui/Barber arXiv:2211.01227, Candès arXiv:2103.09763 (both VERIFIED). NeurIPS census (161093) reports bounds-as-exact does not hurt RMSE.
ranking.rationale: The scout rated this top-tier, but verification shows the core methodological idea (conformal scoring from one-sided/interval bounds) is largely published in the general statistics literature (2501.10117, 2607.02173, 2408.16381). What remains is the MOLECULAR instantiation + benchmark + the decision-relevant one-sided-lower-bound framing -- an application paper, not new theory. Still plausibly publishable in JCIM as a benchmark if framed honestly as 'applying and comparing interval-score conformal to real assay censoring,' but novelty and positive-result likelihood are capped because the general method already guarantees coverage; the contribution reduces to showing drop/impute baselines break and the known fix works. Not the recommendation.
ranking.sharpened_design: If pursued: instantiate interval-score split-conformal (per 2501.10117) on one-sided type-I assay censoring, emphasise the decision-relevant lower-predictive-bound-for-actives quantity and the exact-partial-order scoring that avoids IPCW; semi-synthetic censoring sweep (0/10/25/40%) on TDC ADMET + MoleculeNet for ground-truth coverage, ChEMBL native qualifiers for realism. Baselines: drop-censored, impute-at-threshold, impute-Tobit-mean, bound-as-exact, survival-transplant LPB. RQs tie to: coverage vs censoring fraction, interval width/efficiency, fraction of finite usable lower bounds, decision metric (true actives whose LPB clears a cutoff). Position strictly as benchmark + decision-quality, not novel conformal theory.

ranking.title: Calibration as a leaderboard axis: conformal coverage under scaffold, cluster, and SIMPD-temporal splits, noise-referenced
ranking.closest_prior_art_found: CoDrug arXiv:2310.12033 (real) shows conformal under-coverage under scaffold/fingerprint splits + density fix; KMM-CP arXiv:2603.26415; Tursunbadalov arXiv:2607.06605 (VERIFIED) class-conditional fix; NeurIPS 2025 'CP for Molecular Properties under Label Shift' (neurips.cc/virtual/2025/125228). SIMPD 10.1186/s13321-023-00787-9 (VERIFIED), Ash 2025 (VERIFIED). The conformal-under-shift space is crowded.
ranking.rationale: Feasible and well-scoped but the weakest of the benchmark-axis trio because 'conformal under shift' is heavily published. Its differentiators -- SIMPD temporal arm, noise-referenced interval width (shared with A), and the 'calibration as a reported leaderboard axis' framing -- are real but incremental. Overlaps A on the noise ceiling and C3 on the UQ-decision question. Better folded as a section of A than run standalone.
ranking.sharpened_design: If merged with A: add a calibration axis reporting split-conformal coverage + interval width under 4 splits (random/scaffold/Butina/SIMPD-temporal) for LightGBM/RF wrapped in standard/normalised/Mondrian/density-weighted conformal; reference width to the per-dataset noise ceiling from A; headline = accuracy ranking does not predict calibration ranking. RQs: coverage-gap vs train/test distance; cheap-fix recovery; accuracy-vs-calibration ranking mismatch. Ash paired protocol.

ranking.title: Conformal hit-selection with FDR control that uses, rather than discards, censored calibration labels
ranking.closest_prior_art_found: Bai et al., JCIM 2025, 10.1021/acs.jcim.5c01633 (VERIFIED) = conformal selection, exact labels. Sesia & Svetnik arXiv:2512.18118 (VERIFIED) 'Distribution-Free Selection of Low-Risk Oncology Patients' = conformal selection with FDR via conformal p-values under right-censoring (IPCW); arXiv:2505.04568 conformal survival bands with FDR. Jin & Candès arXiv:2210.01408, 2307.09291 (VERIFIED). The 'conformal selection + FDR + censoring' combination is already demonstrated in survival.
ranking.rationale: More novel-looking than C1 but similarly anticipated: Sesia & Svetnik 2512.18118 already do FDR-controlled conformal selection under censoring. The molecular type-I adaptation (threshold-known one-sided labels, no IPCW needed) is a genuine but narrow simplification. ranking.title: Does any uncertainty signal improve molecular decisions over point-ranking? A 15+ dataset practical-significance audit
ranking.closest_prior_art_found: Srivastava & Kassetty, arXiv:2611.01512 (VERIFIED, Nov 2026) = the 2-dataset/1-model result. Ash 2025 (VERIFIED) protocol. Morger Sci Rep 2022 10.1038/s41598-022-09309-3. MUBen arXiv:2306.10060. No large-scale protocol-grade decision-quality-vs-ranking audit exists.
ranking.rationale: Valuable evaluation-validity question and CPU-feasible, but risks being read as 'just scaling Srivastava' and risks a largely negative/confirmatory result JCIM reviewers may find thin without a constructive deliverable. The decision-rule output ('when UQ helps, when ranking suffices') is the needed differentiator. Positive-result likelihood is only moderate because the most likely finding is 'UQ rarely beats ranking,' which is publishable but softer than D's or A's concrete quantitative headline.
ranking.sharpened_design: If pursued: >=15 datasets x >=3 model families x 3 calibration-provenance regimes (random/scaffold/temporal); measure realised coverage/FDR vs nominal and whether gating/abstaining on each UQ signal (CP width, Venn-ABERS, ensemble variance, kNN-AD) beats point-ranking on precision@budget/BEDROC/enrichment, with Ash effect sizes and win/tie/loss vs the ranking null. Deliverable: decision-rule + reusable CPU benchmark. Pre-register to avoid scope creep.

ranking.title: Leakage-controlled, compute-matched re-evaluation of pairwise/delta learning
ranking.closest_prior_art_found: DeepDelta J Cheminform 2023 10.1186/s13321-023-00769-x (VERIFIED) -- crucially, its own design already pairs molecules AFTER CV splits so 'every molecule occurs in train-pairs OR test-pairs, not both,' which pre-addresses the strongest leakage claim. DeltaClassifier 10.1039/d4md00325j (VERIFIED). Nelen J Cheminform 2025 10.1186/s13321-025-00956-y (VERIFIED). SQRL arXiv:2501.09103 (VERIFIED) already shows similarity-thresholded pairing matters. CliffSplit arXiv:2605.17265 (VERIFIED) cliff-aware evaluation.
ranking.rationale: The headline leakage premise is partly defused by DeepDelta's published split design (molecules already separated across train/test pairs), so the train-anchored pairing regime is not actually how DeepDelta evaluates -- the leakage decomposition may find little. The surviving contributions (compute-matched budgets, decision/ranking metrics, SQRL-style pairing sensitivity) are legitimate but incremental, and SQRL/CliffSplit already probe adjacent questions. Lower JCIM distinctiveness than D.
ranking.sharpened_design: If pursued: three test-pairing regimes (all-pairs/train-anchored/within-test) to isolate augmentation vs leakage; cap delta training pairs to the absolute model's compute budget; add lead-op decision metrics (within-series Kendall tau, top-k analogue accuracy, sign accuracy) across 30 MoleculeACE + ~10 TDC regression sets; Ash paired protocol. Frame as 'when does pairwise help' characterisation, not a takedown.

ranking.title: Coverage for unseen chemotypes: hierarchical/Mondrian conformal prediction with new-group guarantees over scaffold clusters
ranking.closest_prior_art_found: Lee, Barber & Willett arXiv:2306.06342 (VERIFIED) hierarchical-exchangeability new-group coverage theory. Dunn/Wasserman/Ramdas arXiv:1809.07441. Rakhshaninejad arXiv:2505.18890 (cluster-conditioned CP for DTI, SEEN groups). CoDrug arXiv:2310.12033, KMM-CP arXiv:2603.26415 (scaffold covariate-shift CP). No scaffold-cluster instantiation of hierarchical new-group CP found.
ranking.rationale: The new-group guarantee is a real distinction from covariate-shift CP, and the scaffold-cluster instantiation is genuinely unfilled. But the likely empirical outcome -- hierarchical new-group intervals are valid but very wide, needing many clusters -- caps practical appeal, and the space reads as 'yet another CP-under-shift' paper. Needs a demonstrable usable operating point to clear review.
ranking.sharpened_design: If pursued: Bemis-Murcko/Butina clusters as exchangeable groups; split hierarchical CP calibrated at group level for held-out-cluster coverage; compare marginal/within-group-Mondrian/covariate-shift-weighted/hierarchical; characterise width-vs-validity and minimum cluster count for nominal new-group coverage. >=15 TDC/MoleculeNet + MoleculeACE sets. Report where scaffold-cluster exchangeability holds.

ranking.title: Conditional-coverage recovery at activity cliffs via roughness/AD-conditioned Mondrian conformal prediction
ranking.closest_prior_art_found: Research Square rs-10071162 (UNVERIFIED; search indicates a single high-school-author supplement -- treat as weak/unreviewed) already proposes neighbour-roughness + roughness-conditioned CP on all 30 MoleculeACE targets with the same coverage-stabilisation result. MoleculeACE 10.1021/acs.jcim.2c01073 (VERIFIED). Oršolić dAD 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad465, Hosni 10.1021/acsomega.5c11875, Tursunbadalov arXiv:2607.06605 (VERIFIED). Srivastava arXiv:2611.01512 (VERIFIED) suggests abstention/gating gains over ranking are often cosmetic.
ranking.rationale: Kill. The core idea is already laid out in an existing (if unverified) preprint that this would formalise and extend -- high scoop risk and the formalisation (Mondrian-on-roughness = group-conditional coverage) is a modest wrapper on known machinery. Narrow scope (cliffs only), and Srivastava's negative result makes the decision-benefit likely cosmetic (coverage traded for width with no downstream gain). Would require independently reproducing the base claim before any contribution, and even then the ceiling is low. If the cliff theme is wanted, D is the far stronger way to own activity-cliff evaluation.

recommendation: PURSUE D: the pairwise, leakage-audited activity-cliff metric for MoleculeACE. It is the single best risk-adjusted bet: fully self-contained (30 cached datasets, no external noise-ceiling assumptions or custom losses), cheapest to run (~5-7h on 4 cores, well inside budget), targets a verified gap (no MoleculeACE cliff-partner leakage audit or pairwise cliff metric exists in the literature), corrects a highly-cited JCIM benchmark on its home turf, and is structurally defensible even if accuracy ties because the contribution is evaluation validity (exactly JCIM's stated priority per Ash 2025). It is double-hypothesised so it cannot collapse to a pure null: either MoleculeACE's official splits leak cliff partners (a 1-NN/scaffold-lookup memoriser control will expose this almost by construction) OR the pairwise sign/ranking/delta-magnitude metric re-ranks the method pool relative to per-compound RMSE_cliff. Either outcome is a publishable headline, and 30 single-family datasets deliver real multi-dataset statistical power. Runner-up is A (noise-ceiling re-ranking), equally strong on JCIM fit and headline impact but carrying more dependency risk (ChEMBL replicate sparsity, ceiling-estimate uncertainty, and a 'this extends Crusius' objection); if D's leakage audit comes back thin, A is the fallback, and the two share a noise-ceiling estimation module so some work transfers.\n\nWHAT WOULD MAKE D FAIL: if (a) partner-leakage across the 30 sets turns out negligible (MoleculeACE's spectral-cluster-then-cliff-stratify splitting may already separate most cliff partners) AND (b) the pairwise metric yields essentially the same method ranking as RMSE_cliff, then both headlines evaporate and the paper becomes a weak confirmatory null. Secondary failure mode: cliff-pair-disjoint re-splitting shrinks the already-small training sets so much that apparent method differences vanish for trivial data-size reasons rather than leakage, confounding RQ3. Mitigations: pre-register both hypotheses and the 1-NN memoriser control (which surfaces leakage even at low rates); run the metric-concordance experiment (RQ2) independently of the leakage experiment so the paper stands on either leg; and include explicit training-set-size controls plus repeated-split variance in RQ3. Avoid over-claiming a universal leakage problem -- frame as an audit + a corrected, task-matched metric, and verify the MoleculeACE JCIM DOI (10.1021/acs.jcim.2c01073; the Crossref lookup returned only the SI record 10.1021/acs.jcim.2c01073.s001 and the chemRxiv preprint 10.26434/chemrxiv-2022-mfq52, both verified) before submission.
